title: Reach Flipped the Ranking: Intercom’s Three RICE Examples, Scored With and Without the R
text: Medium RICE vs ICE: Intercom's RICE Examples, With and Without Reach | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in The two frameworks, side by side Why McBride split Impact in two McBride’s three projects, scored The same three, minus the R The window is a decision too Where each one fits A Reach checklist for any scoring sheet Sources Product Management Prioritization Startup Product Strategy Growth Reach Flipped the Ranking: Intercom’s Three RICE Examples, Scored With and Without the R Sean McBride’s RICE and Sean Ellis’s ICE look like cousins. Put them side by side on McBride’s own numbers and one letter changes which project ships first. Andrei-Nicusor Covalescu 7 min read · 1 hour ago -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by Natalia S on Pexels Two people named Sean. Sean Ellis, who founded GrowthHackers, gave growth teams ICE: Impact, Confidence, Ease. Sean McBride, writing on Intercom's blog about how his product team prioritised, gave product teams RICE: Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort. The acronyms differ by one letter, so they are often treated as the same tool with an extra column. They aren’t. Put them side by side and the differences sit in the units, the arithmetic and, above all, in that extra letter. This piece does exactly that, using only the three worked examples McBride published in "RICE: Simple prioritization for product m anagers" on the Intercom blog. (ICE itself got its own walkthrough here in an earlier piece on scoring growth experiments , so this one stays on the comparison.) The two frameworks, side by side What each letter asks. In the GrowthHackers vers ion, written up by Anuj Adhiya on the team’s official Medium publication , Impact asks how impactful you expect a test to be, Confidence asks how sure you are that it will prove your hypothesis, and Ease asks how easily you can launch it. RICE asks how many people a project will affect in a set period, how much it will affect each of them, how confident you are in those estimates, and how many person-months it will take. Scales. ICE grades each criterion from 1 to 10 and, in the GrowthHackers write-up, presents the average. RICE uses different scales per factor. Reach is a raw count "per time period," ideally "from product metrics." Impact is multiple choice: 3 for massive, 2 for high, 1 for medium, 0.5 for low, 0.25 for minimal. Confidence is 100% (high), 80% (medium) or 50% (low), and anything below is a "total moonshot." Effort is whole person-months, or 0.5 for anything well under a month. Arithmetic. ICE averages three numbers. RICE multiplies three and divides by the fourth: Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort. McBride describes the result as “total impact per time worked.” What the score means. Adhiya calls ICE “a system of relative prioritization," explicitly not meant to be precise. A RICE score carries units. If Reach is customers per quarter and Effort is person-months, the score is roughly impact-weighted customers per quarter for each person-month spent. Designed for. ICE grew up in weekly growth meetings, where GrowthHackers says each member nominates up to two ideas and the team greenlights three to five tests a week. RICE was built for a product roadmap, with McBride's own team counting customers "over a single quarter." Why McBride split Impact in two McBride opens the post with four ways prioritisation goes wrong. It is satisfying to work on pet ideas you'd use yourself instead of projects with broad reach. It is tempting to chase clever ideas instead of ones that hit your goals. It is exciting to start new ideas instead of ones you're already confident about. And it is easy to discount extra effort. Each RICE factor is aimed at one of those biases. Reach is aimed at the first. In his words, it exists “to avoid bias towards features you’d use yourself.” That explains the split. In ICE, a single Impact score has to hold two different things: how many people a change touches and how much it changes things for each of them. RICE pulls those apart. Reach becomes a count you can look up. Impact becomes a judgement about one person. The judgement stays fuzzy, but the count no longer hides inside it. McBride’s three projects, scored Here are the inputs exactly as the post gives them. Project 1. 500 customers reach this point in the signup funnel each month, and 30% choose the option, so Reach = 500 × 30% × 3 = 450 customers per quarter. Impact 3 ("huge" for each customer who sees it). Confidence 100%, because reach comes from metrics, impact from user research and effort from an engineering estimate. Effort 2 person-months. Project 2. Every customer who uses the feature each quarter sees the change: Reach 2,000 per quarter. Impact 1. Confidence 80%, as reach and effort are supported but impact is uncertain. Effort 4 person-months. Project 3. A one-time effect on 800 existing customers, with no ongoing effect: Reach 800 per quarter. Impact 2. Confidence 50%, because reach and impact may be lower and effort higher than estimated. Effort 1 person-month. The current version of the post gives these inputs and the formula but doesn’t print the final scores, so the arithmetic below is a reconstruction. It is simple multiplication: Project 1: 450 × 3 × 1.0 ÷ 2 = 675 Project 2: 2,000 × 1 × 0.8 ÷ 4 = 400 Project 3: 800 × 2 × 0.5 ÷ 1 = 800 Project 3 wins, despite the lowest confidence. It is cheap and touches a lot of people. The same three, minus the R Now delete Reach and keep everything else. This is not an ICE score (ICE uses 1-to-10 grades and an average), but it shows what happens when a team rates impact per person and forgets to count people, which is the slip RICE was designed to catch.
